function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script) to finish the task.  
I’ve also included the exact files that should end up in the repository so you can verify the output before committing.

> **NOTE** – The helper functions in the “Tools” section are only meant for generating Dockerfiles/Kubernetes YAMLs for *Python* projects.  
> Since this repository is a **Node.js** application, I’ll hand‑craft the files instead of calling those helpers.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# Make sure you have SSH access set up for GitHub
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create artefacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Assuming the repo contains a standard `package.json` and an entry point called `app.js`, the Dockerfile below uses the official Node 18 slim image, installs dependencies, copies the source, and starts the app.

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Stage 1 – Build
FROM node:18-slim AS builder

WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source
COPY . .

# Stage 2 – Runtime
FROM node:18-slim

WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy built artifacts from the builder stage
COPY --from=builder /usr/src/app .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * Uses multi‑stage builds to keep the final image small.  
> * Installs only production dependencies (`npm ci --only=production`).  
> * Exposes port **3000** – the default for many Node/Express apps (adjust if your app uses a different port).  

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a single file `k8s/deployment.yaml` that defines both a Deployment and a Service. Adjust the image name/tag to match your CI/CD pipeline later.

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- update with real registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys 3 replicas (adjust as needed).  
> * Exposes the app via a `ClusterIP` service on port 80, forwarding to container port 3000.  
> * Uses a placeholder image name – replace with your actual registry/tag once CI builds the image.

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. This workflow:

1. Checks out the repo.  
2. Sets up Node 18.  
3. Installs dependencies.  
4. Builds the Docker image.  
5. Pushes the image to GitHub Container Registry (GCR).  
6. Optionally runs tests (you can add your own test step).

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write   # Needed to push to GHCR

    steps:
      - name: Checkout repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '18'
          cache: 'npm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test   # <-- adjust if you have a test script

      - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          IMAGE_NAME=ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome
          docker build -t $IMAGE_NAME:latest .
          docker push $IMAGE_NAME:latest
```

> **Important**  
> * The workflow uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` to authenticate to GHCR.  
> * If you want to push to another registry (e.g., Docker Hub), replace the login/action and image name accordingly.  
> * Add any additional steps (linting, coverage, etc.) before the `docker build`.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

---

## 🎉 Done!

Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run on every push to `main`, building and publishing the Docker image.  
If you have a Kubernetes cluster, you can apply the manifests with:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
```

Feel free to tweak the replica count, image tags, or environment variables to suit your deployment strategy. Happy coding!
